utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, will you have the accused brought in? (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can everyone hear me? Yes? Mr. Blaskic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLASKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning counsel. Good morning, your Honours. I would like to call as my next witness Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you get up, please? Please tell the Tribunal your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic from Vitez, a specialist in internal medicine and occupational medicine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are now going to read the statement that has been given to you. You must have before you a text in your own language which is the solemn declaration that you are requested to read. Can you read it, please? DR MUHAMED MUJEZINOVIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, the Trial Chamber thanks you and you can now answer the questions put to you by the Prosecutor. You may be seated. Mr. Prosecutor? Examined by MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning Dr. Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you spell your last name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am Dr. Muhamed, Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you spell your last name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: M-U-J-E-Z-I-N-O-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How old are you, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 18th May 1949 in the village of Vrhovine, municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a specialist in internal medicine and occupational medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe your educational background for the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in Vitez in 1964, to continue my education in a secondary medical school in Sarajevo, which I completed in 1968. After that, I enrolled at the Faculty of Medicine in Sarajevo. I joined the Yugoslav People's Army to do my military service in 1975/76. Upon my return from service, I graduated from the School of Medicine in Sarajevo and my first job as a doctor was in the medical centre in Doboj. In 1979, upon the invitation of the authorities in Vitez at the time, Dr. Franjo Tibold, who was also Director of the health centre, I went back to Vitez to work there as a doctor, and I worked there throughout until the present time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you in addition to your professional responsibilities as a doctor at the health centre held any voluntary medical positions in the community of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the community of Vitez, after working for a year there, I became doctor of the medical centre in Vitez, and I was then sent to specialise in internal medicine, and I completed my specialisation in 1984. After that, I worked in the medical centre in Vitez and in the general hospital in Travnik. In 1979, I completed a second course of specialisation in occupational medicine and occupational diseases, and I did post-graduate studies in labour capacity in Sarajevo. In addition to my professional activities as a doctor, I was active in all the sports clubs in Vitez as a doctor. I also worked occasionally for the International Red Cross, especially giving lectures for prospective blood donors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, having lived in the Vitez community most of your life, I would like to ask you to describe what life was like in the Vitez municipality before the start of the war, what life was like between the various ethnic groups in the community.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitez is a small industrial town with very developed sports activities, and in the urban part of the municipality there were about 5,500 inhabitants and in the surrounding villages, which mostly had asphalt roads, electricity supply, telephone lines, there was a total of 28,000 inhabitants. The rate of employment was very high in Vitez; there were more than 8,600 people employed. I said that Vitez was a town where the standard of living was relatively high in our circumstances in those days. I am not aware of any interethnic incidents in Vitez ever since my arrival there in 1979 until 1991, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you have described in respect of peaceful coexistence between the various ethnic groups, was that also true in Busovaca municipality and Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was. I never heard of any interethnic strife. People from all over the former Yugoslavia worked in Vitez. We had a special purpose industry, we had a large number of technicians and engineers from Macedonia, Slovenia, Serbia, Croatia, but the local experts were, of course, in the majority. As I said, I never heard of any interethnic incidents in the area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to turn your attention to the late 1980s and the early 1990s and ask you: did political parties emerge in Bosnia in that timeframe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 1990, we had only one party. In 1990, several political parties emerged, among them three nationalist parties. In Vitez, there was the Croatian Democratic Community, the party of democratic action, the Serbian Democratic Party, the League of Communists, the party of democratic reform, the alliance of reform, changes, the Union of Socialist Alliance of Democratic Changes and the Democratic Union of Socialists. There was also the Croatian Party of Rights which did not participate in the elections in 1990 as far as I know. There were eight parties in Vitez in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify the major nationalist political parties that operated in the Vitez community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The nationalist parties -- the main nationalist parties were the Croatian Democratic Union, the Party of Democratic Action, the Serbian Democratic Party and the Croatian Party of Rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to focus your attention initially on the HDZ political party. Was that the political party of the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HDZ was the party of Bosnian Croats, but it was based in Croatia, in Zagreb. It was part of the HDZ and the party itself was a part of the HDZ from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, can you identify by name only the main political leaders of the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Vitez; that is right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1990, the President of the HDZ was Anto Valenta. He was a graduate technologist. Then Pero Skopljak, a Master of Theology, Marijan Skopljak, Ivica Santic, also a graduate technologist. I think that they were the main politicians in the party of the Croatian Democratic Community in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning now to the SDS party, was that the party of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the party of the Bosnian Serbs. Its President was Jovica Mijatovic, a medical technician from Vitez, and the vice-president was Zero Slobodan. I think he was a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning next to the SDA party, was that the party of the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, was the party of Bosnian Muslims. Its first President was Hajrudin Karic and a year later, elections were held in the SDA in Vitez, and the second President was Munib Kajmovic, professor of history in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, you said there were also some minor political parties that functioned in the Vitez community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you identify each of those parties and their leaders, and at the same time, Dr. Mujezinovic, could you also identify if they were associated with any particular ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The League of Communists, the party of democratic changes, its President was Nevin Karadzic; the Union of Socialist Youth, the Democratic Union, its President was Asim Sibro. The Union of Reformist Changes, the Reformist Party, the President was Suad Salkic, a graduate engineer, electrical engineer. The Democratic Union of Socialists, its President was Josip Silic, a professor from Vitez. Those were the parties which were not nationalist, and which mainly fostered the traditions of the prewar parties, some to a lesser, some to a greater extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a role in the SDA political party, and if so, can you describe what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until August 1991, I did not have any role in the Party of Democratic Action. At the elections in August 1991, I was elected to the executive board of the SDA for Vitez, and as the first vice-president of the party for Vitez. Actually, that was when I joined actively in the work of the party. Until that date, I never took an active part in politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your duties and responsibilities in that particular capacity as the Deputy President of the Municipal Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the absence of the President, I would stand in for him on the Executive Board. My activity in Vitez focused on the formation of humanitarian and cultural societies in Vitez in 1991. That is how we formed the Muslim humanitarian organisation Merhamet and the cultural society of Muslims, Renaissance. In addition to my professional duties and the other activities I engaged in that I have already described, I took an active part in the work of these newly-formed cultural and humanitarian societies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an official position in Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was the vice-president of Merhamet, and also in the cultural society of Muslims, I was also the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just explain briefly what Merhamet was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Merhamet is a humanitarian organisation whose policy was to help the elderly, the frail, the refugees, the displaced persons, people in need of relief, to help them find accommodation, clothing, food, education, medical treatment. Those were the programme objectives of the Merhamet. It was linked to the network of Merhamet societies throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and beyond Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that we had organisations in Rijeka, Split, Zagreb, Maribor, Ljublijana; in Germany, Austria, Switzerland. This was a purely humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to turn your attention to the cultural and art association, Preporod. Can you briefly describe to the court what activities that organisation engaged in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our aim in Vitez was to reactivate the culture of Bosnian Muslims, to revive folklore, poetry, literature, through public fora. As it operated only briefly we held in Vitez only two performances, at which writers and poets performed, and we collaborated with the Croatian cultural society Napredak, of which I was also a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, I was going to turn to that area next. Did the Bosnian Croats have similar charitable and cultural organisations and, if so, could you identify them by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Bosnian Croats had the charitable organisation in Vitez called Caritas, and a culture society of Bosnian Croats called Napredak. As far as I know, they had the same programmes as the charitable and cultural societies of the Muslims. We co-operated with both Caritas and Napredak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of one of those Croatian cultural or charitable organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the cultural society of Bosnian Croats, Napredak, the President of which was Zvonimir Cilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there essentially meetings between the two, collaboration between the two cultural organisations and charitable organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cultural society Preporod and Napredak -- I had worked in Vitez for many years and we were together active in sports and preventive activities, so we agreed on joint actions, joint performances. Unfortunately in Vitez we organised only one such joint event. We had the well-known poet from Sarajevo, Dzamahudin Lazic and Zeljko Ivandic who made guest appearances in Vitez, and this was jointly organised by us. As the war broke out shortly after that, we did not have any further opportunity nor the necessary conditions to further this co-operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, I would now like to turn to a different topic and that is the elections that were held in the Vitez municipality. First of all, could you tell us when they were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not actively involved, but when I had time, I attended the public rallies of all the parties. The elections were held in November 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the results of those elections? If you could, could you identify the number of seats that were won by each of the respective political parties that campaigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Municipal Parliament, or Assembly as we called it, had 60 delegates or representatives in it. The majority of seats were held by the HDZ, 23; they had, 23 seats. The SDA, the party of Bosnian Muslims, had 16; the Serbian Democratic Party had 2; the League of Communists, the party of democratic change had 9; the party of -- the reformist party had 7; the Democratic Union of Socialist Youth had 2, and the Democratic Union of Socialists, 1 seat. There was a total of 60 deputies in the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the elected deputies formed a governing body, the Municipal Assembly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the functions of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly had authority and its President from the HDZ, Ivan Santic, was President of Parliament and he convened the Parliament as necessary by the orders, decisions and conclusions adopted by the Municipal Assembly. All other institutions in the municipality were guided by those decisions and that applies to the municipal government, the police, the defence, the economy. In fact life as a whole and the organisation of life in Vitez was run by the Municipal Assembly or Parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the head of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The head of the Municipal Assembly was a representative of the HDZ, Mr. Ivan Santic, a graduate technologist from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a Croat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an Executive Board or President of the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that the Parliament, the Municipal Assembly, was the authority that issued orders, and the municipal government or the Municipal Executive Board had executive power, and it was chaired by Mr. Fuad Kaknjo, an electrical engineer from the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaknjo was a Muslim, that is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly, can you explain the relationship between the Municipal Assembly and the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The new assembly, or rather the new government was set up and started operating only at the beginning of 1991. During the first year of its work, I do not know of any problems that existed between the Parliament and government and their mutual relationship. The Parliament did its job; the government did its job. Of course, there were certain disagreements which was only natural, but all decisions were carried through. There was very good co-operation between the President of the Municipal Assembly and the President of the government in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did the Municipal Assembly convene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Municipal Assembly. The President of the Municipal Assembly convened the Assembly when necessary. I really do not know how often they met. I was not actively involved because I was not a member of the Municipal Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have on the easel a photocopy of what is exhibit 45 and I would ask that that be marked as Prosecutor's exhibit 45B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Has this been admitted? It differs from 45, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I am going to use this with this particular witness and have him make markings on it and then ask that it be admitted as 45B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, would you please approach the large photograph that is on the easel, and with a green pen, would you circle the buildings where the Municipal Assembly met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the building of the Municipal Assembly in Vitez (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mark a circle in green around those buildings, please, Dr. Mujezinovic? Where is the Municipal Assembly building in relation to the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Across the street is the hotel Vitez. Do you want me to circle that too?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that is all right. You can take your seat again, Mr. Mujezinovic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is the hotel and this is the post office in Vitez. This is the hotel and this is the post office (indicates).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you Dr. Mujezinovic. You can take your seat again. Earlier in your testimony, you identified some significant individuals who played a role in the HDZ political party, one of whom was Anto Valenta. After the elections in Vitez, what role did Anto Valenta play either in the party or in the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Anto Valenta has a degree of technology. He worked as a teacher in the Vitez High School and he held the post of President of the HDZ for Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, did Anto Valenta assume a greater role in Herceg-Bosna affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later on I think in the latter half of 1992, I think that Anto Valenta left the post of HDZ President to Mr. Pero Skopljak, and Anto Valenta became the Deputy President of the HDZ of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did Pero Skopljak play in Vitez's political and civil affairs after the elections in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pero Skopljak worked in Vitez as the head of the municipal police, the MUP or SUP. He did this professionally in Vitez and he was also on the Executive Board of the HDZ for Vitez. I do not know about other posts he held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it, Dr. Mujezinovic, that you first became aware of Herceg-Bosna? Can you explain that to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the Municipal Parliament, at the end of November 1991, it was said that a cultural community of the Bosnian Croats was established, and the club of Members of Parliament of the SDA reported to us about this at the meeting of the Executive Board of the SDA in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was reported to you, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was reported to us that the President of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Ivan Santic, mentioned at the Municipal Parliament that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established as the cultural community of the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any mention about the Vitez municipality becoming part of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The delegates of the SDA, as we were told or as I was told, asked what that meant. Ivan Santic answered then at the Assembly that this is only a cultural community of the Bosnian Croats, and that in no case, under no circumstances, would it jeopardise other ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina or the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Also the delegates of the SDA reported that at the Municipal Parliament, some time in March 1993, they put the question again as to what the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was, and they reached a decision that the status of the municipality of Vitez could be changed only if the Municipal Parliament passed such a decision by a two-thirds majority vote, if this would be adopted by the Municipal Assembly and we were told that this was adopted unanimously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just testified a moment ago, Dr. Mujezinovic, that the delegates of the SDA reported at the Municipal Parliament in March 1993 that they put the question as to what the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was. Was that in March 1993 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992, I am sorry. I am sorry, slip of the tongue. 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, how long did the Municipal Assembly remain in existence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, we asked or we insisted at the Executive Board of the SDA -- we insisted with the Members of Parliament that the Assembly be continued. As far as I know, the last Municipal Assembly of Vitez was held some time in March, the beginning of March 1993, and it was not held again -- 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, March 1992 the Municipal Assembly ceased to exist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not work any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What took its place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the Executive Board of the SDA, the President of the SDA party for Vitez, Mr. Munib Kajmovic and the President of the Executive Board of Vitez reported to us that the Croatian Democratic Community proposed that a Crisis Committee for the municipality of Vitez be established, because we had a lot of problems in Vitez. We had a lot of refugees and there was a war going on around us. We accepted that, to have a body established which would work faster, which would be smaller and which would reach decisions on behalf of the Assembly, but this Crisis Committee, this body, would have to be verified officially by the Municipal Parliament. That was some time in January, at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you use the words "Crisis Committee", is "Crisis Committee" synonymous with the term "Crisis Staff"? Let me ask the question again. Dr. Mujezinovic, do the terms "Crisis Committee" and the "Crisis Staff" mean the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about Crisis Committee. I know about a Crisis Staff only, but it can be a synonym really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Muslims agree with the formation of a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The representatives of the SDA party agreed to that, that a Crisis Staff be established in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the ethnic composition of the Crisis Staff, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Crisis Staff, at the beginning, there were only representatives of the SDA and the HDZ. There was parity; there were five Croats and five Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Bosnian Serbs represented on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but they were invited from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify the members of the HDZ political party who were members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The President of the Crisis Staff was Mr. Ivan Santic. Another member was Mr. Anto Valenta, Pero Skopljak, from amongst the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Marijan Skopljak a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Josip Silic, Pero Skopljak, that is, Anto Valenta, Josip Silic, Vlado Santic, and the President was Mr. Ivan Santic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify the members of the SDA, the Bosnian Muslims who were members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the SDA, there was Munib Kajmovic, President of the SDA party, Fuad Kaknjo, President of the Executive Board for Vitez, I was there, then Sulejman Haseli and Hakija Cenjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff eventually expand to include representatives of important industries and factories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Later the Crisis Staff was joined by the director of the biggest factory, Mr. Krizanovic, Nikola, and Mr. Vlado Divkovic and Zfikret Hajdarovic, an engineer from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your role in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My role in the Crisis Staff was to organise the medical staff under war conditions, so I was in charge of the medical staff under conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do to fulfil that particular obligation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got an assistant, Dr. Bruno Busuk, a dentist, to work together with me, and if necessary we could ask other medical doctors and workers to join us. At that time in Vitez, we made a reserve location for the Dom Zdravlja in case of war. Also we renovated the cellar of a motel in Kruscica so that these premises could be used to take in wounded people or injured people. My role was also to lecture on first aid in different local communities, or self-assistance in cases of massive injuries and wounding. Through work organisations in Vitez we did this, or rather humanitarian organisations in Vitez, we had done this pretty well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did the Crisis Staff meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff met whenever necessary, sometimes very often, sometimes even every day. When there were problems, we would meet very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you would meet, would it be a meeting of all the representatives from the SDA and from the HDZ political parties; in other words would the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims meet on almost a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were in contact every day, because it is a small town, but we also met officially whenever needed and as a rule, all would be present. Mostly all of us were present. If somebody would not come, a replacement would always come in from that particular field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Generally, how long would these meetings last, on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended on the current problems. Sometimes for about a hour, sometimes for about four or five hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would the Crisis Staff govern? How did it implement its decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff took over the function of the Municipal Parliament, the municipal government. Actually, it was the main authority in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the Crisis Staff reached a decision that related to police affairs would it inform the police authorities and the police authorities would then implement the decision of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that also true with the other functions of government, with finance, with education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the Crisis Staff continue to function? When did it cease to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff operated until mid-June approximately, or more precisely 18th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning your attention back to the meetings between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims' representatives on the Crisis Staff, during some of those meetings, were threats made by the Bosnian Croat representatives to the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At a meeting of the Crisis Staff some time in April, or the beginning of May -- I cannot remember exactly when; I cannot remember the exact date -- Mr. Anto Valenta, then in the capacity of President of the HDZ in Vitez, made it known to the representatives of the Bosnian Muslims or the representatives of the SDA that in Vitez they would have to be under the authority of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. On that occasion, he advised and warned the representatives of the Bosnian Muslims not to put up any resistance, because the Bosnian Croats in Vitez are armed 90 per cent, and the Bosnian Muslims, according to his estimates, are armed to an extent of about 10 per cent, and he mentioned the information of HOS, that they existed in Vitez then, but they were negligible. We did not take it seriously at that point. I even had the impression that other representatives did not take him seriously either; rather the representatives of the HDZ. At that meeting Mr. Ivan Santic commented that Mr. Anto Valenta always makes jokes, but he said, "I am speaking very seriously and I am warning you", and that ended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that meeting took place either in April or May. Was that in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that particular threat was made by Mr. Valenta, did the situation between Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims remain harmonious, or did things begin to deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you quite frankly, we were very worried by this, we in Vitez. In that period, in the first half of May, there was not a single excess incident. The first such incident in Vitez was on 20th May, when a soldier of the BH-Army was killed in the hotel Vitez, and two soldiers were captured, and badly beat up. That was the first excess incident between the HVO, and then the TO, the Territorial Defence in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to examine any of those soldiers who had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I examined two soldiers who were not beaten up, but badly abused. They had bruises on their bodies, on their legs, on their backs, they had haematoma that were all together, blended into one another. They were not individual haematoma, so that is the kind of injury they had sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of that incident, did the Bosnian Muslims request that an investigation be conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivan Santic convened an urgent meeting of the Crisis Staff. He called me after midnight, and when we came, he told us that a soldier of the Territorial Defence had been killed, that two soldiers were captured, and we asked him to clarify things to us, to tell us what was happening. This was done by the commander of the HVO for Vitez, Mr. Mario Cerkez. Three soldiers were in the hotel Vitez, they came into the restaurant that was in the cellar of that hotel, and they were provoking other people and when they were walking out of the hotel, they were killed by the guard who was guarding the hotel. Vukadinovic Miro was the name of the guard. At the Crisis Staff it was agreed that the captured soldiers of the HVO be given to the military police of the TO, the Territorial Defence, and start an investigation of this killing. Also it was concluded that the family of the killed soldier be told about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was to tell the family of the killed soldier what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a medical doctor, I talked to Mr. Ivan Santic; he was rather influential and popular in Vitez. I asked him to come with me to tell the family about this. He refused that. He said, "You Muslims work this out amongst yourselves." So I waited in front of the hotel with Mr. Fuad Kaknjo and the Commander of Police, Saban Mahnutovic. I waited for the captured soldiers to be returned and to be handed over to the TO military police. I asked the Commander of the Military Police of the HVO in Vitez how this had happened. He told me briefly, "Doctor, can you not see that Mario Cerkez is drunk? At the meeting, Mario Cerkez was half drunk. He went out and he shot a soldier." I do not know why he did it, but we put the man into the car; he was dead already but we took him to Travnik hospital”. Later, we went and told the family about it, some time during the night. At 2.00 or 3.00 am we told them that the soldier had lost his life, and then we asked again whether the captured soldiers had been brought in. The captured soldiers were brought in only the next day around 1.30, or rather they were released only the next day. As I said, they were badly beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had received information that Mario Cerkez, who is a Bosnian Croat, had been the person responsible for the killing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was informed that by his Commander of Military Police, Ivan Budimir, who was a coach of the football club and a teacher of physical education in Vitez, a very nice and very popular man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What role did Mario Cerkez play in military affairs in the Vitez community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was introduced to us as the Commander of the HVO, the military formations for Vitez; that is the HVO brigade of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, was an investigation ever concluded into the killing of this particular Muslim soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, the investigating magistrate in Travnik instructed the Prosecutor, Vlado Miskovic from Vitez to carry out an investigation, but the investigation was never completed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it Mario Cerkez was never arrested or prosecuted for that particular killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The soldier, Miro Vukadinovic, who was a guard in the hotel at the time -- he simply disappeared from Vitez. We heard that he was somewhere in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, you said that the Crisis Committee ceased to exist on 18th June 1992. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what occurred on 18th June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 18th June, in the afternoon, there was unrest among people, and I asked my neighbours, "What is up?" On 18th June, military formations of the HVO captured the police headquarters in Vitez, and the Municipal Assembly building. They raised flags of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the flags of the state of Croatia. I asked Mr. Fuad Kaknjo whether he knew what was happening. I called him up by phone. We were neighbours; he lived in the same building. He said he did not. We went together to the staff building, the Commander of the TO was Cenjic Hakija and on the way, we met a group of HVO soldiers in full combat gear with helmets. One of the soldiers was employed in the health centre and I asked him, "Miro, what is happening?" He said to me, "Go, flee, doctor; it is war. There are snipers, somebody will kill you." Then we asked the Commander of the TO, Hakija Cenjic whether he knew what was happening and he said he did not. He just said military formations had captured the police building, the Municipal Assembly building, that they had hoisted these flags, the flags of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and of the state of Croatia, without the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina having been hoisted. At that moment, Ivan Santic, the President of the Crisis Staff, was not in Vitez. He was also President of the Municipal Assembly. He was away on business somewhere, I do not know where. Three days later, at the meeting of the Executive Board of the SDA, Kaknjo Fuad, the Prime Minister, informed us that Mr. Ivan Santic had invited him to go and do his job, that of the Prime Minister, that he had promised to take down the flags and that the army would withdraw from the police building and from the Municipal Assembly building, and that the police officers of Muslim faith who happen to have been -- who were employed at that moment would be reemployed and that their weapons that had been seized from them would be returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Prosecutor, somebody said "Prime Minister". That is the first time I hear this name of Prime Minister. Can we make a clarification of this point, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Mujezinovic, there appears on the translation the term "Prime Minister". I think it probably came up twice, Prime Minister in respect of Fuad Kaknjo. Fuad Kaknjo was not the Prime Minister, was he? I think there is an error in translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the Prime Minister. He was the President of the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are using the term "President of the government" and "Prime Minister" synonymously.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does that clarify it, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned, Dr. Mujezinovic, that in a meeting some three days later there had been a promise made by, I think, Mr. Santic that the Muslim police officers who had been disarmed and lost their jobs would again regain their positions and be given back their weapons as police officers. Did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A couple of days later, they were taken back to work, their weapons were returned to them, they started doing their job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did they remain in their jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They remained until about 20th October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that date, did they lose their jobs permanently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you just a couple of questions. The municipal building where the Croatian flag and the Herceg-Bosna flag were publicly displayed, that is the set of buildings that you have circled in green on exhibit 45B; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is across the street from the hotel Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 18th June, when the HVO seized power in the Vitez municipality, were there any announcements on radio and television as to what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was announced on radio and television, but at the official meeting of members of the Crisis Staff, we addressed the question as to what was happening, what is going on. We did not know at the Crisis Staff meeting, and then at the time Mr. Anto Valenta, as the President of the Croatian Democratic Community, told us that this had been done by an informal armed group, and Mr. Pero Skopljak, who was Acting Chief of Police, commented with the words that the Croatian people in Vitez did not have the patience to wait for problems to be solved and they were beginning to take things into their own hands. After that, it was said that it was not the Crisis Staff, the Parliament, the municipal government that had been elected in November 1992 that was to govern, but a new government, an HVO government, the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that repeated on radio and television; that is that the HVO was now the government in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the leaders of the HDZ political party appear publicly on television or radio to make such announcements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not watch that on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any comment or discussion about Vitez being part of historic Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was mostly Anto Valenta who said that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had been formed already before, and that it was not a cultural community of Croats but an area comprising about 30 municipalities, that it was an economic, political, cultural and defence entity of the Bosnian Croats, and that that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the sphere of interest, or the zone of interest, of the Bosnian Croats, that it was the historic right of the Croatian people that vital interests were involved, and that the representatives of the Croats would use all available means and resources to struggle for the realisation of that goal. They again called on the representatives of the Muslim people who had been elected at the free democratic elections in November 1990 to take their seats in the newly-formed, one-nation government. We refused to do that, because we felt at the time that only the legally-elected government can function, and not any single nation government imposed by force. We made it clear that the sovereignty and the legitimacy of the state and the local authorities and the state had been violated, and, in view of the fact that there were no marks of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but rather the flag of the Croatian municipality of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian state, that this was an assault on the territorial integrity of Bosnia and the annexation of a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, perhaps we can have a break now and resume work at 11.40. The hearing is adjourned. (11.20 am) (A short break) (11.40 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please bring in the accused. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us continue, please, with Dr. Mujezinovic. Mr. Prosecutor, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Dr. Mujezinovic, before the break I was asking you about statements that had been made about historic Croatian land and you were discussing with us statements that were made by Anto Valenta. Will you please continue with your testimony in that respect. Dr. Mujezinovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Before the break, you were testifying about statements made by Anto Valenta. Could you please continue with your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At joint meetings, mostly attended by former representatives of the Crisis Staff, Pero Skopljak demanded that the demands of the Croatian Democratic Community be carried out, and that a joint civilian authority be set up with the participation in the government such as to reflect the democratic elections in 1990; that army units in Vitez had to place themselves under the command of the HVO; and that the command structure of the HVO should include the same number of representatives of the Muslim community in accordance with their percentage share in the units; that the civilian police should be placed under the command and in the service of the newly-formed government, and that it should not follow the instructions of the Republic MUP, but rather the instructions of the newly-formed Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Pero Skopljak made it clear that 50,000 well-armed HVO troops supported this, that the whole of Croatia was behind this, and, as he put it, the western democratic-minded public opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, let me ask you, at the same time that these comments were being made, were there additional comments that were threatening to the Muslims? Were there additional comments being made by other leaders of the HVO and Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain those comments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Central Bosnia, other places such as Travnik, Busovaca, Novi Travnik, were having similar problems. Parallel with these local negotiations, negotiations were organised at the regional level, the level of the Travnik region. I participated in Busovaca, Travnik, Novi Travnik, and a statement by Dario Kordic, who was introduced as the Vice-President of Herceg-Bosna, and an HVO Colonel, were to the effect that they denounced the policies of Alija Izetbegovic and the Muslim leaders. I even recall a TV programme when Dario Kordic stated, and this was somewhere around the beginning of March 1993, that the Muslims would disappear from Bosnia and that Bosnia-Herzegovina would disappear thanks to the policy of Alija Izetbegovic and the Muslim leaders. Similarly Ignjac Kostroman at those meetings and over the local media threatened, saying that these were historic Croatian lands, that the Croats are ready to correct historical errors, that they had been exploited in these parts, humiliated, and that now they had the power and the strength for the Croatian people to win their rights, their historic rights, to assert those right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Ignjac Kostroman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ignjac Kostroman was introduced to us as the Secretary-General of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this same time period after the HVO seized power in the Vitez municipality, did Mario Cerkez make any threats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At joint talks, the HVO formations in Vitez were always represented by Mario Cerkez. For a time, but in the first half of 1992, he would attend meetings -- meetings were attended also occasionally by Mr. Filip Filipovic, who was in Vitez in the first half of 1992. In fact Mario Cerkez promised that the HVO had the strength and the power to put into effect what was expected of them, and that in the process they would not spare effort or means to attain their goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, after 18th June 1992, when the HVO became the only executive body in the Vitez municipality, what did the Muslims do for their own protection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Leading question, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Objection rejected. Continue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez, at the free democratic elections in 1990 in Vitez, only 60 per cent of the Muslims had voted for the SDA party. At a meeting of the Executive Board of the party, we felt that we did not have the right, on behalf of the whole Muslim community in Vitez, for us to decide; we did not have the right to decide on behalf of all the Muslims, so we convened a meeting of all the political representatives, people of prestige in Vitez, of Bosniak nationality, and we put to them the question as to what the others thought about it. At that meeting, which was held on 12th July, the policy of the Croatian Democratic Community was denounced; the single party government in Vitez was denounced; a conclusion was adopted to the effect that the Bosniaks in Vitez would not respect the decisions and orders of such a government. They would respect only those decisions which were in conformity with the law, with the decisions of the Municipal Assembly, and the decisions of the Presidency of the republic. The proposal was made that a body be set up which would monitor the work of the newly-formed government in Vitez, and it was called the Co-ordination Committee for the Protection of the Interests of the Muslims. It was an association which had 19 members. 13 of them were given specific assignments to monitor the interests and any violations of the interests in various areas, and we agreed to issue public announcements. This body did not have the characteristics of a government. We thought and sought an agreement to set up a joint authority at the level of the municipality, and we initiated a meeting on a broader scale at the level of the municipal boards of the HDZ and the SDA in order to deal with these problems, and one such meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to that meeting, Dr. Mujezinovic, can you tell me specifically what various sectors in the community of Vitez were monitored by members of the Co-ordination Committee for the Protection of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, there were 19 members on this Committee, people who were directly involved in monitoring finance, education, health, revenues -- actually, everything in Vitez, sports activities, cultural activities, humanitarian activities, defence activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the monitors supposed to do, based on information they observed or received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were supposed to present that at these meetings, and then we were supposed to make our views public through the media at local, regional and republican levels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you selected as one of the monitors, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was elected for monitoring health, because I am a doctor. I was involved in health, to see how Bosniaks were treated by doctors and what kind of medicine they were given, how elderly people were treated by doctors et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, was there a leader of the Co-ordination Committee for the Protection of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Chairman of this Co-ordination Committee for Protecting the Interests of Muslims was Fuad Kaknjo, President of the Executive Board, the municipal government, and Fuad Kaknjo and other officials of the Bosnian Muslims, Muslims who worked in municipal institutions, received instructions to continue working in the government that was elected in 1990, in November, and they went to their offices regularly, they went to work every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Co-ordination Committee for the Protection of Muslims have contacts with the Bosnian government on the republic level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We only issued statements, and through Fuad Kaknjo as the Prime Minister, he was in charge of contacts at regional and republic levels before and after; that is to say contacts with the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Co-ordination Committee for the Protection of Muslims receive any advice or direction from the republic level or any elected leaders on the republic level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we issued statements asking them what to do, because we had a lot of problems, and that is why we addressed not only the public at home but also the international public, international humanitarian organisations, the UNPROFOR, the UNHCR and that is what these statements were aimed at. We directly addressed everyone, you know, through these statements. We did not have any instructions from republican authorities, but at that level we wanted to have problems that had accumulated resolved, because there were more and more such problems in the organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you collected your information about the various aspects of life for Muslims in the Vitez community, would you present those problems to the HVO government and try to seek a solution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me how that worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to give an example, temporarily I was director of the Dom Zdravlja in Vitez because my predecessor had left this, Dr. Dzevald Balta. He did this by way of demonstration because he said he had no conditions to work properly. In the Dom Zdravlja, it is the worker's council who appoint the director. I was asked to take over this post before a new director was elected. I used an official car. One day, the military police of the HVO simply came and said, "Hello doctor", and I said hello. "We have been ordered to take away the keys of your car." That is an example. Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic, the acting director of the Dom Zdravlja in Vitez, had his car keys to his official car taken over from the HVO military police, so that is the kind of statement we issued and that is an example of that kind of statement. Should I give you more examples? For instance, a doctor of veterinary medicine in Vitez, who had been working there for 25 or 30 years, an elderly gentleman with three bypass operations carried out on him, he went to work in a village in the vicinity of Vitez; he was beaten up by HVO soldiers. I examined him afterwards and we addressed the public through radio, television -- Travnik television, the joint television, the Sarajevo television -- and we said that a doctor, a veterinarian was beaten up by an HVO soldier in such and such a village near Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you bring that to the attention of the HVO leaders in the Vitez community directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Invariably, they would respond that it was informal, armed groups that did this and that they had no authority, no command over them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Co-ordination Committee for the Protection of Muslims a group that was attempting to create conflict in the Vitez municipality or trying to create harmony in the community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Co-ordination Committee for Protecting Muslims truly tried to create a harmonious life in Vitez. At one of the meetings of the Co-ordinating Committee, the representative -- the President of the Co-ordinating Committee or the Prime Minister, he presented the view of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, that in Vitez we had to iron out our differences with the Croats, that we should not allow a conflict to happen; that in Vitez and in the other municipalities, we can only use force if the physical integrity of people is harmed. It is in that direction that we worked. I personally had a lot of problems with armed Muslims and armed Croats as I did my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, after 18th June 1992, did life become more difficult for Muslims in the Vitez community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The new government introduced a new organisational pattern for the municipality. All the workers who were employed as staff working in the municipality, they had to sign a statement of allegiance to the new government. Whoever did not sign that on 25th November 1992, I think, lost their jobs. We thought that this would extend to work organisations too, to education, health institutions et cetera. The new government introduced new taxes as well. Actually, they took over all the financial resources that belonged to the municipal budget. Just one example: an entrepreneur, a businessman, had to deliver some wooden planks to a business partner in Split, and he asked the HVO to give him a pass and they would not give him one. I went to see Mr. Anto Valenta with Mr. Djidic, who was a teacher in the high school in Vitez; they had worked together. After a three-hour conversation, Anto Valenta told us, "There is no problem for this person to take these wooden planks to Split, but you have to accept the new organisational pattern of the HVO authority in Vitez, HVO government, otherwise he will not be issued a pass", and we could not get this pass for him so that he could do his business. Kislajmovic is the name of this person, a prominent businessman who has a private firm of his own in Vitez, but this was valid for all others. If they did not have passes to get through HVO checkpoints, they could not get through and Central Bosnia had only one road that led to the rest of the world. That road went through Novi Travnik, Busovaca to Dalmatia; that is to say that everything else was blocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there increasing problems at HVO checkpoints for Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw with my own eyes, when individual soldiers of the HVO, because there was a civilian police of the HVO and there were members of the HVO army, not two or three of them only but a group of 15 or 20 people. They had machine guns, they were well armed. I saw them take cigarettes from a woman who would be carrying, say, two packs of cigarettes; they would take one pack and leave her one. At these checkpoints there was general robbery of money, and people were beaten up and their cars were taken away from them; private cars and vehicles carrying goods. We, the Co-ordinating Committee for Protecting the Interests of Muslims in Vitez, we always made our views public on such matters when we would find out about these things. At the checkpoints it is not only the people of Vitez who were robbed but also people who were passers-by, people who were going from Tesanj Doboj, Sarajevo. We were asked by them to help them get back their goods or their weapons or whatever from the HVO authorities. Sometimes we would succeed in doing so but not always, and as time went by it became increasingly difficult to get these goods back. I do not know if ever any such person was held accountable by the HVO government, either the civilian or the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is after you made complaints to the HVO government about what had occurred at the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you quite frankly, I had the impression that they were fooling around with us. I will tell you a story. When my own car was taken away, my children came in from the street to say that HVO soldiers had taken away my own car. As a citizen of Vitez, I first went to the HVO civilian police to report this. Then I went to the military police and then they started laughing and saying, "Look at this fool! Is he crazy or is he a fool?" Then I went to the police of the BH-Army and they registered it to the other civilian police. After seven days Croat and HVO soldier came to me and told me who took my car away. He promised he would get my car back for me. It never happened. I can tell you here the name and surname for example, Peko Garic, an HVO soldier who enjoys a good reputation in Vitez, and his family too. He told me that a group of HVO soldiers from the village of Ovlat took my car away and that he would personally make an effort to have my car returned to me. I did not get it back. There were many such cases in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 18th June 1992, what happened to Muslim-owned businesses and shops in the city of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time in October, there was a conflict in Novi Travnik. In Vitez, the situation became increasingly complicated. I was the doctor on duty in the general hospital in Travnik the weekend of the 17th and 18th, and on the morning of the 19th the wounded from Novi Travnik were brought in. I came to Vitez to do part of my job, and I went to my home. In the morning, when I was leaving for work, in front of my house, Omeric Anto, a Croat, my neighbour, he said, "Doctor, do not take your car, the HVO soldiers will take it away from you." I asked why. He said there was a conflict in the village of Ahmici. I went to work, and as acting doctor of the Dom Zdrvalja, I was told that the HVO army, Mario Cerkez and the BH-Army did not agree on military problems and that they were expecting a conflict. We moved to the reserve location of the Dom Zdrvalja and we were waiting. That day in Vitez, we saw four or five wounded Muslims from Kolonija who came in for treatment, and Bruno Buzul, my colleague, who was my deputy in the Dom Zdravlja, kept warning the medical staffs, "No, do not go out", because Muslim snipers were shooting from roofs, and we kept receiving wounded civilians, Muslims, in the Dom Zdrvalja. When this stopped, some time after that, there was massive destruction of facilities in Vitez, and people were beaten up. One of these people came to me for treatment and examination; Ibrahim Hodzic is his name, I did not know who had destroyed his cafe but he came beaten up. A neighbour of his, a Croat, Ruzic Stipo brought him in, and he just said HVO soldiers came. They broke up his cafe, they beat him up and they threw him out. After that, in Vitez -- it is a small town, you know -- I saw that many cafes were destroyed. When I asked how many, the public security service, or rather the police, told us that during a day or two about ten such establishments were destroyed, those that were owned by Muslims in Vitez. We intervened, and the question was always put, time and again, but formulated in a different way, the conditions on which the situation would become calmer in Vitez, putting the army units under HVO command, the civilian authorities, the civilian police too. In that period, as far as I can remember at one of the meetings they even showed that, in order for the situation to calm down in Vitez, the Deputy Commander of the operative zone of Central Bosnia, Mr. Tihofil Blaskic would guarantee this, but the conditions were the same for the situation to calm down after that. I am talking about the month of October, and the beginning of the month of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, would you approach Prosecutor's exhibit 45B, which is the large photograph on the easel? With a yellow pen, would you please put a circle around the apartment building where you lived? Would you put a circle with the yellow pen around that building, please, Dr. Mujezinovic? That building represents your apartment building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can take a seat again for a moment, Dr. Mujezinovic. From your apartment building, did you see any shops destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, in October, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about any time after 18th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the later period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain to the court what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One evening, some time around 1.00 or 2.00, we heard detonations. My wife and I and my father and mother-in-law were staying with us and we got up to see what was happening. A group of soldiers -- I think this was 20th January -- was simply throwing grenades in the street and breaking windows, shop windows, with their rifles. I can show it to you if you want.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please take the red pen that is in front of you, Dr. Mujezinovic, and will you mark on Prosecutor's exhibit 45B the location of those buildings that you saw being damaged or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, these buildings (indicates) and also here, this is where the town pharmacy was, and they continued along this street later, and then here they destroyed a building too, this same group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a butcher's shop that was destroyed as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at the same time, you know. This was during the night, around 2.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do we not stay with this particular set of observations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the butcher's shop was in this building, which was destroyed, I do not know, about a day earlier, but in the afternoon, and we watched this from our window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do we not take the first series of observations that you made, Dr. Mujezinovic. You said you saw soldiers throwing grenades into buildings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could hear detonations, I could not see them, it was dark, until they came in front of my building. Then we saw them and they woke up all the tenants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following day, did you go out on the street and observe any damage that had not been there the day before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One evening, in the second half of January, about 10.00, a terrible detonation was heard in the morning. In the morning, I saw that here, the commercial bank of Travnik was destroyed (indicates). In the evening, some time around 10.00. Simply all the windows were shattered, there was a terrible detonation, and all the glass on the windows was broken and also on the neighbouring building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the significance, Dr. Mujezinovic, of that particular bank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commercial bank of Travnik at that time used the official currency in use in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, as far as I can remember, we had already started to receive coupons or Croatian dinars as our salaries, because I was still working. This bank was still operating with the dinar of the former Yugoslavia or the previous Yugoslavia, whichever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only bank in Vitez that was dealing with the Bosnian or Yugoslavian dinar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the only bank in Vitez with the exception of the Zagreb bank which was opened very close to it, but I think it never actually started operating, at that time at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, you mentioned that you observed a butcher's shop being destroyed. Can you explain to the court what time of the day that occurred and where the butcher's shop was located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The butcher's shop was owned by the work organisation Zmajevac from Zenica. This was a state-owned enterprise. It was across the way from my apartment building, and around 5.00 in the afternoon, I had come home from work, my neighbour called us in to our bedroom and the children's room to see how the butcher's shop was being broken up by a group of HVO soldiers. My neighbour recognised another neighbour of ours whom we called Gulag; his name is Crnic Drago, who with a group of soldiers was simply breaking up the windows and carrying out everything he found inside, the choppers, the knives, the refrigerators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, by the time of the start of the conflict in April 1993, how many Muslim-owned businesses and shops were intact in Vitez; that is the parts of Vitez controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was one cafe left owned by Hamo Selimic, I think that was his name, which was intact. That owner was looted; his cafe was one of the better ones. It was not destroyed, but we were told by the SUP that the owner of that cafe, Hamo Selimic, I think, that his cafe is the only private shop that remained intact in the urban part of Vitez, downtown Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, did most of the destruction of these shops take place by grenades, by bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the formation of the HVO government, since it was our task to try and calm the situation, that part of Vitez was under the absolute control of the HVO, both the civilian and the military police, and when we asked the HVO government or the civilian police that we carry out an investigation on the spot together, this was not allowed. The police were not allowed, the police of the Bosniaks, which was under the control of the republic's MUP, could not carry out an investigation. For example when the bank was blown up, when the Krivaja premises were blown up, there was an accident when a young boy lost his life, but an investigation was never permitted. That was how we were informed by Saban Mahmutovic and Salem Topcic whose responsibility this was. One of them was Chief of Police and the other one was Chief of the Criminal Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, Dr. Mujezinovic, could the detonations that caused the damage to those Muslim shops that you have described be heard from the hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the hotel Vitez is maybe 300 metres away. I do not know whether it was even that far. It is very close to that spot. I do not know exactly, but it is not far. Those detonations could be heard throughout Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, was life also difficult for Bosnian Croats who did not agree with the policies of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many of them complained, you see. I personally saw Croats who had been beaten up by the HVO. One day I was sitting in the SDA office with my associates, and the President of SDP, Neveka Rajic, and her secretary Suada Akeric, ran in asking us to help. When we went out, HVO soldiers were beating with rifles two Croats who were members of the SDP. One was called Stipo Brkan and the other one Mijo Ivanic. I examined those people. After they were treated Stipo Brkan did not behave normally in the street any more, and the others too had problems. The going story was: who was not in favour was against, and he would get what is coming to him and that meant he would be beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a third member of the SDP party who had also been beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zdravko Livancic came to me to be examined. He had been beaten up. I asked him, because I knew the man well, "So what happened? Tell me." He was a first class captain in reserve. He used to work in the TO staff; he was a well-built young man and not stupid at all. "How did you get these?", I asked, and he told me he had been beaten up by the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he had been beaten up by the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he just said that he had openly criticised the HVO policies. I think that he was beaten several times on that account. I think he was even imprisoned, but I am not sure about that, but he did come to me for an examination when he had been very badly beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, how long did the Committee for the Protection of Muslims exist and when did it cease to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992, a decree was passed by the Presidency of the republic that districts should be formed, and within that framework -- the War Presidencies -- and since we had initiated on a number of occasions meetings with HVO representatives, and made our proposals as to how the bodies of authority should be formed in the Vitez municipality. One of the proposals came from a Croat, Josip Silica, who had a good reputation in town, that this should be called the Croat/Muslim Defence Council. This was accepted by everyone at the time, and three or four days later Fuad Kaknjo, the President of the government, and Munir Kajminovic, the President of the SDA party, informed us that nothing would come of those decisions because the HVO government had not received approval from Grude. There was another occasion when we agreed to form a wartime government of Vitez. The main problem was the preamble, how we would call it. We in Vitez did not want it to be a single nation government, and to be coloured ethnically and, since we did not succeed, an initiative was launched that a War Presidency be formed of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it created?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was created on 15th January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were its members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 15th January 1993, the members of the War Presidency were representatives of all the Parliamentary parties, as well as the Commander of the Civil Defence, a representative of the army and at that meeting, no one accepted -- I was not a Member of Parliament, but no one accepted to be President of the War Presidency. I was proposed, but I too did not accept. They tried to persuade me, saying that I had to accept, that I have very good relations in Vitez with everyone and that is true; that I would succeed in appeasing the situation and that we would avoid conflicts in Vitez. I accepted that on 2nd February 1993, even though I was warned by the Croats, some Croats who used to be close to me, that this was stupid, and that I would get killed as a result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, just to clarify your testimony, were Croats participants in the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the War Presidency remain in existence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The War Presidency was active until October 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the legal basis for forming the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decree of the Presidency of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, was the War Presidency a parallel form of government, parallel to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain what authorities, what powers it exercised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It had again the right to issue orders, conclusions, instructions, which applied to the army, the police and the civilian organs of authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it have the equivalent of ministers, for example somebody who controlled the health portfolio, somebody who controlled the education portfolio, the defence portfolio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
