utterances.text: No, it was a smaller body, but we also had a wartime government which had these portfolios. The War Presidency is a smaller body, and its orders, conclusions and decisions were implemented by the government and the appropriate ministers, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the War Presidency issue orders to the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to a part of the army. Its competencies included -- for instance in Vitez a brigade was formed at the end of 1992 from the soldiers in Vitez, but its main command in the military structure was in Zenica, the Third Corps there, so we had a defence staff of Vitez, and they had a command in the district staff in Zenica. My authority and that of the War Presidency was to propose who would be the Commander, and the Commander had the right to appoint his own members of his staff, and all our orders -- for all our orders they had to consult the higher level command, and we had authority over the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Prosecutor. Could you please ask the witness to repeat -- I apologise to the witness too -- his answer to your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, I asked you whether the War Presidency could issue orders to the military. Could you again answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they had to get approval from their own military command, which was based in Zenica, that is the Third Corps there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, if the War Presidency issued an order to the military, it still had to be approved by the Third Corps in Zenica; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the members of the War Presidency, including yourself, meet with members of the HVO government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you meet with the HVO government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We continued to work on the establishment of joint bodies of authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would you meet with the representatives of the HVO government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a doctor, I was very frequently, almost daily, in contact with Ivan Santic, Pero Skopljak, Valenta, Marijan Skopljak and the others, you see. When I took over as President of the War Presidency, at that time, there were conflicts going on in Busovaca. Vitez was under blockade at the end of January, so we agreed with HVO representatives that we would respect all the decisions of -- observe all the decisions taken at a higher level, and in that sense, through the mediation of international organisations, UNHCR, UNPROFOR, the European monitoring mission attached to the UN, a meeting was scheduled between the Commander of the operative zone of Central Bosnia and the Commander of the Third Corps. We agreed that whatever agreements were reached would be observed, and a joint order was issued, I think it was about the 15th February. A commission was formed but it was all nicely written, you see. Then there would be a lull for ten or fifteen days, and then it would start again as before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "it would start again", what is "it"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am referring to the incidents, mistreatment, looting, confiscations, breaking into people's houses, physical beatings, robbing of money, arresting of prominent Muslims, intimidation, blowing up private houses in town, burning of houses, killings of wealthy people, businessmen. One of the richest Muslims in Vitez was killed in front of his house and his house robbed; another one on the way out of Vitez. They called me to do the investigation, and my colleague, who was a Croat who would come to Vitez occasionally from Zenica to work there -- when he returned from the investigation, he told me that what he saw was terrible. A person was killed and then a grenade was thrown in that tore apart his body and his house, so there was nothing for me to see, he said, but bits of his body strewn around. That is what I am referring to. For example, in Vitez, we had a very good electrical engineer who is an honorary citizen of the city of Zagreb. He was a winner at the quiz on television; at night a group of HVO soldiers broke in. The man had three little girls. They beat him up, they looted him, they said, "You have lots of money because you won that award in Zagreb, that prize." Another case, a doctor of technology, the leading engineer in the manufacture of explosives and gunpowder -- in daytime a group of HVO soldiers with stockings over their heads took him out of his house, in front of his children, then they brought him back beaten up, and then in the middle of the night people would break in and beat up people and threaten them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO ever resolve those problems to the satisfaction of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not recall. You see, at the time, my impression was that this was being further fanned. There were written documents promising safety, but the basic precondition was that a joint authority had to be formed under the control of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, a joint military command under the command of the HVO, a joint police, according to the decrees of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and at all the talks we had this was the starting point and this was the conclusion. But the promise was that things would calm down, these lootings, mistreatments of Muslims, prominent Muslims, would stop, as well as the devastation of private homes, private businesses, the eviction of refugees. We did not choose who would come. I had 17 refugees from eastern Bosnia in my own apartment. I did not invite them there, they came. The comments made on local HVO television by Ante Marijanovic -- he made comments saying that the Muslims in Vitez were pursuing a sly policy, that they were settling people in Central Bosnia so as to win over power at the next elections. That is why those people had to be expelled from Vitez so as not to change the population structure, and each refugee had to have a Red Cross card to register and to receive humanitarian aid. I can tell you of an example. I think it was 12th or 13th April in 1993. I said that I was Vice-President of the charitable society Merhamet for Vitez. Representatives of the International Red Cross came to see us and ask us why 400 refugees had left Vitez in three days, and this was happening on a daily basis. People were being robbed. They were asking why these refugees were fleeing Vitez. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have one additional question before the break, your Honour. You mentioned the name Ante Marijanovic. Who is Ante Marijanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ante Marijanovic at that time was editor on the local HV television; I think he was one of the editors at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. I have no additional questions at the moment. I will continue after the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed; please be seated. Bring in the accused, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we are continuing with your interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I start with having Mr. Dubuisson take exhibit 80, and I would ask the usher to put two of those photographs on the ELMO. Mr. Dubuisson, if you could take Z2/456, please, and place that photograph on the ELMO. Dr. Mujezinovic, to your right there is a photograph on the ELMO machine. Could you take a look at that photograph. Can you identify any of the people in that photograph? If you can, would you take your pointer and put your pointer on the figure or figures who you recognise. You have to point on the machine over here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Ignjac Kostroman, secretary-general of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hold your pointer on each individual for just a couple of seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Ignjac Kostroman from Vares, the secretary-general of the Croatian Democratic Community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, can we hear the name well, please? The translation is having some difficulty, so could the name be stated very clearly, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kostroman Ignjac, secretary-general of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. As far as I know, he is from Vares, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dario Kordic, Deputy President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Dario Kordic, Deputy President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. A Colonel, according to his military rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you move to the figure you can identify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Anto Valenta, the first President of the Croatian Democratic Community for Vitez, and later the Deputy President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, born in Dolac near Travnik. For quite some time he lived and worked in Vitez, about 30 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the usher could move to the next photograph which is Z2/457, and place that on the ELMO. Please proceed, Dr. Mujezinovic, and identify the figures you identify in that particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Anto Valenta, with a degree in technology. He worked in Vitez in the high school, a teacher, the first President of the Croatian Democratic Community for Vitez and later the Vice-President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This is Mr. Pero Skopljak, holds a Master's degree in theology. He worked in Vitez for some time as a priest. He came back to Vitez in the 1990s. I did not know him while he worked as a priest, but I knew his family, his brothers and the rest of the Skopljak family. He was the head of the police, MUP, in Vitez in the first half of 1991 and the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, your Honour, Dr. Mujezinovic is pointing to a man who is in the centre of that photograph and is wearing what appears to be a gold-coloured, short-sleeved shirt. Could you move on and identify the next person you can identify in that photograph? I think we have to have this photograph refocused to get a bigger view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Ivan Santic. In Vitez, they called him Ivica, an engineer of technology in Vitez, very well known as an active sportsman. He established the pingpong club, table-tennis club, in Vitez. He was very popular, well liked in Vitez. In Vitez, he was elected President of the Municipal Parliament of the Municipal Assembly, Ivan Santic or Ivica Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, your Honour, in photograph 457 Dr. Mujezinovic has been pointing to the individual in a blue, short sleeved, T-shirt on the right side of that photograph. Thank you Dr. Mujezinovic. Claudius, I am finished with those photographs. The exhibit can be reassembled. Dr. Mujezinovic, while you were a member of the War Presidency and while you were meeting with members of the HDZ who you have identified in these particular photographs, did you continue, you as a representative of the Muslim people, to receive threats from those particular representatives of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at official meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe those threats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On several occasions, Anto Valenta, the Vice-President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, threatened that Vitez was within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and that they, I mean the Croats, this is their historical territory, and that they would do that by force or by resorting to any other means. He said that they had with them the HVO, 50,000 armed soldiers, and Croatia on their side, and privately, when we would meet, he would always say that we should accept the proposal of the HDZ in Vitez, namely to accept the HVO government in Vitez. Pero Skopljak also on several occasions said that the decisions of the HVO government in Vitez had to be carried out, otherwise we would fight, as he would point out, Ivan Santic, only in the second half of 1992, at one meeting, said, "Regardless of whether you accept this or not, in Vitez it is the stronger that will rule." Once in April 1993, Santic invited me to his home and he said that his wife was ill. I went there with my wife to his apartment in Vitez, which was not far away from my apartment. Privately, I asked him to use his influence, because what could a normal person expect after everything; there would be chaos in Vitez. On that occasion Ivan Santic told me and my wife, "I wish I had that kind of influence to prevent that. I am powerless." That is about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Anto Valenta, did you ever see him wearing an HVO uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anto Valenta was most often in HVO uniform. I hardly ever saw him in civilian clothes, as opposed to Santic who always wore civilian clothes. I never saw Santic wear a HVO uniform. Pero Skopljak I would see in camouflage uniform while he was head of MUP, the police, but he often wore civilian clothes too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In conversation with the HDZ representatives you have identified, did they ever make comments or remarks about receiving orders from Grude or Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, Ivan Santic, when he proposed to establish a War Government of the municipality of Vitez, he proposed that we sent to Sarajevo documents saying "Republika Bosnia-Herzegovina, War Government of the municipality of Vitez to Sarajevo and to Grude to send documents Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the War Government of the municipality of Vitez. Of course, this was not carried through, you know. We had agreed to one such variant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, I would like to turn to another topic now and that is refugees who came into Vitez municipality prior to April 16th . Can you explain to the court the situation in respect of refugees in your community, prior to the start of the conflict on April 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many refugees came to Vitez. As I said, the urban area of Vitez did not have more than 5,500 inhabitants while the municipality had a population of 28,000. The first refugees that came to Vitez came in from Croatia, Foca, Sid and Ilok. They were of Croat nationality; they were registered with the municipal Red Cross. They mostly came to stay with families and family homes. The second wave of refugees came from eastern Bosnia and western Bosnia, from the areas of Foca, Tjentiste, Rogatica and the western part of Bosnia. They came from Sanski Most, Sana, Zenica, Kljuc. We registered these people with the Red Cross, and through the humanitarian organisations, Caritas and Merhamet, they received food, clothing, footwear, medicine, and we sought shelter for them. We sent them to families which would take them in voluntarily, and we asked people from Zenica, Vitez, Travnik, who had weekend houses, as we call them -- we asked them to have these people stay in their weekend houses. At any rate, there was a major wave of refugees that came in from Jajce, Croats and Muslims some time in November, I think. Anto Valenta talked to them at the stadium. I do not know how many of them there were, about 7,000 of Croat nationality, but there were also some Muslims among them. There were difficulties in the registration of refugees came about when the HVO government in Vitez simply prohibited the President of the Red Cross, Sead Cajnic and his secretary to enter the premises. They took their keys, their seals, and the HVO government of Vitez appointed Stipo Krizanac President of the Red Cross of Vitez. Keys and seals were taken away from Sead Cajnic. Thanks to Stipo Krizanac, because as he told us, it was no longer allowed to register Muslim refugees, but he continued doing so, although not for all who came in. The largest number of refugees we had registered was about 4,200 or 4,500, I cannot remember exactly any more, but I mentioned already April, March, the people were leaving Vitez then, even in January, because they were feeling less and less secure in Vitez, because of provocations, beatings and looting and robbery by HVO soldiers who came from I do not know where. They were not from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, I would like to turn your attention to the conflict in April 1993. I would like to focus your attention on April 15th, the day before the conflict, and ask you first off, did you go to work that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perform the normal duties at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me what happened on 15th April while you were at work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of the patients that I had been following for a long time were surprised to see me working, and they asked me, "Doctor, the situation is no good. You should leave Vitez." Nobody told me why the situation was no good. I asked for a meeting of the War Presidency, and I asked for a report from the Commission to which we had sent a report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for just a minute. Those patients who you were just mentioning, were those Muslim patients or Croat patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you finish your work in the health centre on 15th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 1.00 pm I left the health centre Dom Zdravlja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your conversations with these Croat patients, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the offices of the War Presidency. I requested an urgent meeting of the War Presidency and of the Commission for Incidents in Vitez. There were three Bosniak representatives and three Croat representatives respectively on this Commission. The members of the War Presidency came to the meeting, together with the Commission which had a meeting with this same kind of commission on the Croat side in the building of the Municipal Assembly. They showed me the minutes from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was President at that meeting, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there, Kaknjo, Munib Kajmovic, Suad Salkic, Sefkija Djidic, Nijaz Sidro and Sifet Sivro, Fuad Zeco.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody there from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a commission. What was the Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Earlier on, following the orders of the Commander of the operational zone of Central Bosnia, Mr. Tihomir Blaskic, and the Commander of the Third Corps of the BH-Army, Enver Hadzihasanovic, at the initiative of international organisations, UNHCR, UNPROFOR, European observers, the United Nations, three commissions were established, three joint commissions which were supposed to work on the ground in order to have the situation calm down. This first commission on the Bosniak side consisted of Sefkija Djidic, Nijaz Sidro and Saban Mahmutovic. I think on the Croat side it was Marijan Skopljak, Samija Mirko, and I do not know who the third person was. They presented their views. This commission presented their views at the War Presidency. They said again there were a lot of incidents and that looting continued at checkpoints, the people were disarmed, their cars were taken, the situation was deteriorating in Vitez. They asked for an urgent meeting with appropriate representatives from the Croat side, and Ivan Santic, Pero Skopljak, Anto Valenta and the Commander of the HVO of Vitez. We agreed to this meeting and the meeting was scheduled for 16th April at 12.00, and we also suggested that these minutes be sent to hotel Tisa in Busovaca where a joint commission was operating of the HVO and the BH-Army, under the control of European monitors and the United Nations. We concluded our meeting around 3.00 pm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the conclusion of that meeting, had you been reassured that nothing was going to happen on 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I forgot to mention that Midhat Varupa was also there and he was given the assignment as a lawyer to call up his colleague Dragan Rados and to tell him we had agreed to the meeting and that we had scheduled it for 12.00 on 16th April, so as to see what the problems were, where we could intervene and try to quieten down the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the meeting, Dr. Mujezinovic, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I did not have my own car, a car of my own, so I headed home on foot, and in front of my house, Zvonko Bekavac was waiting for me. He was one of the members of the HVO government in Vitez, as he said, and he asked me to examine his mother who was sick in the settlement or district called Rijeka in Vitez. I did not go in. I got into his car, a Fiat. I knew his mother well and I had been following her health as a doctor for years. We completed the examination, I issued some medicaments to Zvonko for his mother from the Merhamet supplies as I had the keys on me. After that Vinko Kolak from the village of Jardol came with an elderly man carrying a paper for the hospital, and an X-ray with him, and he asked me to go to the health centre to examine that woman. I finished that and Zvonko took me home. During the night, I was with my family. Many Muslims of Vitez called me up on the phone to tell them what was happening, because the situation did not seem normal in the streets. I kept telling everybody that we had a meeting scheduled for the next day at 12.00 and that there were no problems, that these were just normal activities, but some people answered, "It is not normal." I kept repeating to everyone that we had this meeting and that they had nothing to fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then did you retire for the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What next occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning, about 5.30, between 5.00 and 6.00 am, we were awakened by very powerful explosions. My wife and children, my father-in-law, my mother-in-law, we all got up. I called Sefkija Djidic and asked him, "What is it; what is happening?" He answered on the phone that they had been attacked by the HVO, that houses were burning in Stari Vitez and that there was fighting around the houses. I asked him, "What should I do?" He told me to sit tight and we interrupted the conversation. Just then, somebody rang the doorbell. I looked to see my neighbour, Marinko Katava. We were at the door, my wife and I, and when we opened the door, he told us, "I had warned you that your children should not chant slogans in favour of the BH-Army. You did not listen. You do not exist any more. I have just come to tell you so that you would not be surprised."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in your apartment throughout April 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you observe from your apartment building on 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in my apartment. There were many people who called me up on the phone asking what it was all about, not just from Vitez but from Zenica, from Travnik. There were many provocations; people were asking where was my army; why was I not defending myself? My colleague's wife called me up and informed me that the HVO soldiers had killed Midhat Varupa, a lawyer from Vitez, that she watched it from her balcony. Other people called to say that Nedim Zlotrg and his wife had been killed in their apartment. Then in the middle of the street a civilian policeman, a Bosniak, had been stabbed to death, Salem Topcic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anybody being arrested or being taken out of the apartment buildings near your apartment building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see it at all, I did not dare look. There were terrible explosions and from my living-room and the kitchen I could see the shells falling on the village of Novaci. I sat there and waited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in your apartment building before you actually left the building to go some place else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 8.30 or 9.00, my neighbour, Marinko Katava, appeared again and asked me to go into a room that was empty, and he asked me -- he wanted to tell me what I had done that my life had been saved. I did not understand what he meant. He brought two packs of cigarettes and he told me that it would all be over by Monday -- Saturday, Sunday, Monday -- and that he would tell me who had saved my life and that I was to tell him how one should deal with people in the right way so they would save them afterwards, like I was being saved. After that, a friend of mine, another neighbour, a Croat, an engineer, came. He was crying and he said, "You are saved, just be quiet", and I asked, "Dragan, what has happened to this one and that one?" He just said, "You keep quiet, you have been saved."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, did you remain in your apartment until 19th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in my apartment until Monday, about 10.00, when an HVO policeman, Dragan Calic from Vitez came and told me to follow him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, before we get to the 19th, I just wanted to ask you some questions about your observations from your apartment between 16th April and 19th April. First of all, can you tell me, did you see any damage or destruction from your apartment building when you looked out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the shells falling in the village of Novaci. You could see the explosions; they were falling around the houses. The next day, I saw smoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What day is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vitez, you can see from my living-room. I think it was the 17th or the 18th. I think it was the 17th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the smoke, I saw houses burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you go to the map that is Prosecutor's exhibit 45B and, with a red pen, please, identify the area where that smoke was coming from. You have circled how many areas, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have circled to the right side of Vitez in the immediate vicinity of my house. These houses were burning, the Kavadovic family, then on the other side of the road I could see smoke where Ahmic Dervis, Faik Jadran and Mujkic Edin -- then the Koca family. Anyway, this whole row of 10 or 15 houses inhabited by Muslim families were burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the owners and occupants of those houses, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were inhabitants of Vitez. I knew very many people in Vitez. I knew them well, I knew where everyone lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you said, those were Muslim houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in time, while you were in your apartment building, did you receive a warning of some kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on Sunday around 5.00, Katava Marinko warned us we were not allowed to go out anywhere, because in the hallway there were local people with arms. They were mostly wearing civilian clothes, some of them were in camouflage uniforms with rifles, and we did not move anywhere. Then Marinko Katava warned me and my neighbours, or rather my wife, my children, my in-laws -- he did not talk much to me -- that we should not be afraid, that a strong explosion would be heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Marinko Katava a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Croat from the village of, I think, Kacuni, municipality of Busovaca, who had moved to Vitez to live. He has been living there for some time with his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on that warning, did you or your family do anything in respect of your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we pulled down the windows so that the panes would not be broken. We half opened them because they opened this way and this way (indicates), horizontally and from the top, and my father-in-law opened them in case of a powerful explosion; he wanted to save the windows, so he opened them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there in fact a powerful explosion that occurred shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was dusk. First there was a very powerful light and then a very strong explosion. We did not know what it was and then Marinko Katava said, "Do not be afraid. We have hit Djuda's ammunition depot", as he put it, and Dzevada Topcic, known as "Djuda", held in Stari Vitez a warehouse, and he claimed that an ammunition depot in Stari Vitez had been blown up and that that was the explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn later on that in fact that was not the explosion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later on I learnt actually on Monday when I went to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you learn on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That a tank truck had exploded in Stari Vitez, that many houses had been destroyed, that there were wounded and injured among the people working in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, you said on 19th April, you left your apartment. Did someone come to get you at your apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a military policeman of the HVO, Dragan Calic came. The military police wore those white belts, and my mother-in-law asked, "Where are you taking him?" He said, "Do not worry." As I knew the man -- he said, "Do not worry, we have a lot of wounded, I am taking you to work." I took my doctor's bag and followed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the health centre which was made for wartime conditions, and I had participated in choosing the location -- actually I was the main organiser behind the project, the preparation of medicines, sanitary material, beds, tables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the War Hospital very far from your apartment building, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was in the immediate vicinity, maybe 200 metres away, 250.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the War Hospital, did you have any conversations with any of your staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The nurses who were there were surprised to see me alive. One of them got up, Ruzica Botic. She had worked with me; she kissed me and the others looked on, and there were indeed many wounded people. I put on my white uniform and there were some very young inexperienced doctors working there. We organised first aid; it mainly consisted of first aid. We carried out a selection of those that had to be transported to Travnik, Zenica, Split. I proposed the patients and Bruno Buzuk carried out my proposals regarding the selection of the wounded and their transportation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point while you were at the War Hospital, Dr. Mujezinovic, did the subject of Ahmici come up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 21st October, in that same hospital, they brought in from Ahmici -- they asked us to send an ambulance. The driver of the ambulance who went to Ahmici returned three times because he could not pass. I went home, I was hungry, and a lady doctor, Enisa, asked that I come back quick and I saw Dr. Bruno Buzuk, the lady doctor, nurses and three HVO soldiers who were hitting a civilian wounded man with their legs. They were kicking him and they wanted to take him out and kill him in the street. This was a 55-year-old man who was a businessman, had his own firm, Nesib Kajmakovic. Thanks to Bruno Buzuk alone, we managed to prevent that. The man's left shoulder was crushed; we immobilised his arm, we gave him pain killers and sent him to be treated at the Orthopaedics Department in Zenica. We struggled for him for about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention back to April 19th , 1993. Did the subject of Ahmici come up on April 19th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did not know until then about Ahmici. Two nurses from Ahmici -- one worked with me at the hospital in Travnik; her name is Ankica Tudja. I brought her to the health centre in Vitez to work with me in the specialist ward and another nurse who I did not know from before who had not worked in the health clinic, her name is Santic; she was married in Ahmici; I knew her father, Mate. We know them as Japanovi, this Santic family. Ankica Tudja and this other nurse asked me whether I knew what had happened in Ahmici. I said that I did not. They told me that about 1.00 at night HVO soldiers had evacuated all the Croats from Ahmici towards Lasva and that they had participated as nurses. They started crying, they said to me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It was all the Muslims of Ahmici that were chased out, I think. According to the transcript -- I want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said as follows: that the nurses informed me that the HVO soldiers in Ahmici had all the Croats, the women and children. They had pulled them out of Ahmici towards Donja Lasva and that not a single Croat civilian was left in Donji Ahmici. In the morning about 5.00 or 6.00, Ahmici was attacked and they killed whoever they could: children, women, animals, cows. They told me that it was a most atrocious sight, that the cows were roaming around unmilked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, these two nurses who told you this, were they Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was her demeanour when she was relating this story to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were crying; the nurses were crying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some time on 19th April, did a man by the name of Darko Kraljevic come into the War Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I was brought to the hospital by the HVO policemen about half a hour later, Darko Kraljevic walked in with an escort of three or four soldiers. He was wearing camouflage uniform and he was wearing a big knife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Darko Kraljevic from previous contacts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew the whole Kraljevic family in Vitez, his father, mother, grandfather, uncles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Darko Kraljevic say and do on the 19th while he was at the War Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic said hello to me; he asked me how I was. He addressed the staff, and informed them that I was their chief, their boss and that they had to listen to me. He gave me two telephone numbers, and if there was anything I needed or the members of my staff that I should ask for it, and then he left the premises of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, was Darko Kraljevic a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic formed a unit early on in Vitez called HOS. It is a unit modelled on the units in Croatia of the Croatian Party of Rights. Some time in June my colleagues Franjo Tibold, Dr. Franjo Tibold, and Dr. Zvonko, we were sitting together and having our first coffee in the morning, Zvonko Kajic, and then a nurse came up and called them out and a hour later they came back and told me that Darko Kraljevic had had a heart attack and that I should examine him. Franjo Tibold told me, "Mujezin", we were colleagues so we called each other by first names, "you must go because his people have come. You know what they are like; they will take you there by force", so I went to the house where Darko Kraljevic lived. I examined him, and gave him an injection for detoxification due to alcohol abuse and another one for relaxation. After that, he felt better, and insulted the doctors. Then he came to the health centre for a shot again, and then he told me that he had been replaced, that he was no longer commander, that he would go somewhere for a holiday, that Pero Skopljak and Anto Valenta were persistently forcing him to torch Muslim houses and to provoke chaos, and some 20 days later he told me that he had been restored to a command position, that they were no longer called HOS but Vitezovi and that they were under HVO command, that his forces were not very strong and that he could not resist the HVO in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he mentioned to you, Dr. Mujezinovic, that Anto Valenta and Pero Skopljak were persistently forcing him to torch Muslim houses and provoke chaos, did he mention anybody else by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said "and these others". He did not mention names. Every day -- he would always come with his wife, you know, and his escort was always in the car and we would have to wait until he received his injection in his vein and he would keep me for about an hour and a half in front of the house; he would talk to me. Two or three times his wife was also present, and he asked me what I thought about things and would I leave Vitez, and he said that he did not like what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain at the War Hospital before being taken to another location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed on in Vitez in the War Hospital until 19th May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the War Hospital treating patients, did someone come and take you to a different location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation in Vitez had quietened down. With the exception of the first seven or eight days, there was no fighting any more. From time to time, with the approval of Dragan Petrovic, I was taken to do my doctor's rounds with elderly people, elderly men and women --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, excuse me for a moment. Were you taken at Mario Cerkez's headquarters at some time after you were at the War Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 19th, no -- yes, on the 19th. Two HVO soldiers came some time after 8.00 pm, two military policeman, Anto Kovac, called Zabac by the people of Vitez -- he used to play soccer in Vitez and he was also a soccer judge, and Ratko Nuk, also from Vitez; he was a worker in the SPS factory. I knew them well. They asked for me and I went with them to Vitez, to the "Dom Kulture", the cultural centre, we called it the workers' university, "Radnic Univerzitet", and a cinema hall was there, offices, and the headquarters of all the political parties were also in that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you approach Prosecutor's exhibit 45B, please, and with a green pen put a circle around that location where you were taken? Dr. Mujezinovic, is there a letter inside your circle? If there is, can you just for the record state what that letter is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can resume your seat, please. Dr. Mujezinovic, when you got to that location, who was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In one office, Mario Cerkez was sitting in that office, with Zvonko Cilic, Boro Jozic, Stipo Dzigonjam, Zeljko Rebac, Zeljko Sajevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those people you have identified all members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them were in uniform, with HVO insignia. I knew each one of these people individually and relatively well too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mujezinovic, did you have a conversation -- can you hear me all right with those earphones, Dr. Mujezinovic? Tell us what happened when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez was, I knew from before, the Commander of the HVO forces in Vitez. He asked me whether I was aware of the situation that I was in, and I said that I was, and then he said to me, "Then you have to do what we order you to do." He asked me whether I had heard about Ahmici. I said that I had heard about it. Mario Cerkez repeated that I had to do whatever he ordered me to do. First he said that HVO lines in Vitez were broken through, as he said, in the village of Dubravica from the direction of Zabrdje, and that the BH-Army were advancing, was entering the town towards the chemical factory and was getting into town. He told me that I had to call the command of the Third Corps, to call Alija Izetbegovic, Haris Silajdzic, Ejub Ganic and whoever else I knew, and to tell them that if the BH-Army continued advancing towards the town, that they have 2,223 captured Muslims. He emphasised, women, children, and that he would kill all of them. He also told me that I would have to go on local television, and to ask the Muslims of Stari Vitez to surrender their arms. Finally, he told me that I would have to establish a commission. He gave me a phone, and he said call Zvonko Cilic. I knew the number of Ramiz Dugalic, who was Assistant Commander of the Third Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to that, before Mario Cerkez who made this threat to you, you have identified five other people in HVO uniforms who were present. Were those people present when Mario Cerkez threatened to kill the 2,000-plus prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a number of names that he said you needed to call. One was the Commander of the Third Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One was Alija Izetbegovic who was the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the other people he asked you to call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, as far as I know, Ejub Ganic was a member of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Dr. Haris Silajdzic. I do not know whether he was foreign minister or minister of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then at some point in time a telephone was placed in front of you and did you make a telephone call or a series of telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez told Zvonko Cilic to sit at the same table with me and to do what he said should be done. First, I knew the number of Ramiz Dugalic who was from Vitez, who was a former officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. Vitez was his birthplace and he worked for some period of time in the Territorial Defence of Vitez. I knew all of his family. I called him at the Third Corps and I told him what Mario Cerkez and his command in Vitez were asking for. I repeated that if the BH-Army continued to advance in two directions that they would kill the prisoners. I asked to talk to the Commander of the Third Corps, whom I did not know. Ramiz Dugalic promised that he would call me after he talked to the Commander. After about half a hour, Ramiz Dugalic called me and then I talked to General Hadzihasanovic, the Commander of the Third Corps, and I told him what Mario Cerkez had told me. It was suggested to me to accept everything that the HVO would ask me to do. If they asked me to sign some documents, then I should sign them. I told Cilic Zvonko that and he conveyed it to Mario Cerkez. After about a hour Granic called me. I also called him about this and he suggested to me that I remain in touch with the command of the Third Corps and he said that I should accept, that I should sign officially, if necessary, that the army would not enter Vitez. After that, I was supposed to find a group of Bosniaks to negotiate with the representatives of the HVO government. They told me I had made a list who should be there. Mario Cerkez said, "No, you have down here in the basement about 300 people. Choose whoever you want."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then go down into the basement, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, then I went to the basement with the military police. I was wearing my white uniform, my medical uniform, and I was terribly surprised when I saw people in the heating room where there was still coal. Most of them were from Vitez. Some of them were pensioners who were sick. Among them I chose Sivo Bahtija, an engineer, an electrical engineer, who was a member of the SDA for Vitez; Djidic Kadir, a professor, a teacher from the Municipal Committee of the SDA; Mulahalilovic Nuraga, who was a teacher and director of the secondary school in Vitez; then Fuad Kaknjo, who was President of the government in Vitez, which was elected in November 1990. I said that a young man should come along with me who had an artificial valve implant, Zijad Puric. We came out of the basement and were taken to another office. These offices -- these were the offices of Gerim Muazam, rented for his private firm, the former director of the SPS factory and an electrical engineer. Jozic Boro and Cilic Zvonko were with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, before we go further with what happened in that particular room, I would like you to describe in more detail the conditions that you observed in the basement where these prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a basement. Coal was kept there. There was a big furnace for heating the building, so every winter they would bring in a lot of coal to heat the building. People were simply there on that coal; they could either stand or sit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were there that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told, I did not count them, that there was about 300 people there. I was told that I could choose from among these 300 people a group for negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the conditions overcrowded in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there a number of sick people amongst these 300 people that you had known and had treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Because Zvonimir Cilic had worked as a social worker before in Vitez, I had made a list of 20 chronic patients for him, people who had heart ailments or asthma, that these people should be released immediately because it was suffocating in there, especially for people who had asthma. He took the paper immediately and he said he would see what he could do. I do not know whether they released them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you came out of the basement, you had a list of people who were chronically ill people and you gave that to Mr. Cilic who was in the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You advised Mr. Cilic that those people should be released from custody because of their medical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Mujezinovic, now let us turn back to this group of people who you have selected and taken to another part of the cinema complex. What happened next with those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In one office, with these people, was Zvonko Cilic, Boro Jozic and the two of them, I do not know which one, told these people what they were supposed to do. They were told that they have 2,223 prisoners and that their task was to telephone all their acquaintances and to tell them that if the BH-Army continued to enter Vitez, that these people would be killed, and then they started phoning. I had agreed with Zvonko Cilic that I should go on local HVO television in Vitez to address the public, about 1.00 while these people were making their phone calls. I appeared on local HVO television which was upstairs in that building and I called upon Muslims and Croats not to shoot at each other, because that inflicted harm on both one and the other, and I said, literally, that only Karadzic's Chetniks could profit from that, so that is all I said. This had been shown several times on local television over the next few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, was your appearance on HVO television voluntary or involuntary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was told that I would have to go on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told what you would have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you what you had to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you you had to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To call upon the Muslims in Stari Vitez to surrender their weapons. I agreed with Zvonko Cilic, I told him that nobody would listen to me, and I said what I said. If necessary, I will repeat it once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is not necessary, Dr. Mujezinovic. Your Honour, it is 4.00 and perhaps this would be an appropriate time to take our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, we will resume work at 4.20. (4.00 pm) (A short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed; please be seated. Bring in the accused. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Dr. Mujezinovic, after the television broadcast had concluded, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned to the same room that I had been taken from, where the people elected to the commission for negotiations were waiting for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What occurred next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 2.00, Zvonimir Cilic and Boro Jozic informed those present that if they had finished they could stay in that room to spend the night, or they could go back to the basement. All of us stayed there, with the exception of Fuad Kaknjo, who returned to the basement. We were told that in the morning, about 6.00, Mr. Ivan Santic and Mr. Pero Skopljak would come to have a talk with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they in fact come to have a talk with you the following morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came, not at 6.00 but at 5.00 am, Mr. Ivan Santic and Mr. Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe your meeting with those two individuals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I can reproduce that morning. Mr. Ivan Santic addressed those present with the words to the effect that the HVO government, that is the Croatian Defence Council, had taken the decision, the one I had been informed of by Cilic Zvonimir and Boro Jozic, that they would kill the prisoners if the BH-Army continued to advance. Ivan Santic said that he was very sorry that this had happened, that there were many killed and wounded, but that he did not consider himself to be to blame, but rather Alija Izetbegovic and the Muslim leaders were to blame, because they wanted a unitary state and, as he said, the disillusion of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been completed. I had warned repeatedly the leaders in Vitez, the representatives of the SDA, that the stronger party would rule in Vitez, he said. Pero Skopljak agreed with the previous speaker, and he too said that he was sorry, but that the policy being pursued by the Muslim leaders was unrealistic and unreasonable, and that if the conditions that had been set were not adopted, and he also added that he had said repeatedly that there would be a fight in Vitez because the decisions of the HVO government in Vitez had to be observed and implemented, or rather of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that these were Croatian lands, that Alija Izetbegovic by his unreasonable and unrealistic policy had brought the Muslim people to disaster and possible annihilation. Roughly, that was the message conveyed to all those present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Pero Skopljak repeat the threat to kill over 2,000 civilian prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said that he agreed with the previous speaker, and with the demands of Mario Cerkez, who told me that, and this was told to the others by Zvonko Cilic and Boro Jozic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next, Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivan Santic suggested that an announcement be made from the meeting for the public, and he took out a piece of paper and said, "Here is something that we have put down on paper; do you agree with it?" He read out that paper, that document, and he said that I should sign it and he, so as to calm down the situation and ease the confusion that had occurred in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender as Prosecutor's exhibit 86 a copy of a document. It has attached to it, your Honour, a French translation and an English translation. (Handed). Dr. Mujezinovic, do you recognise Prosecutor's exhibit number 86?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the joint statement which Ivan Santic proposed to me and the group of people who were with me in the building of the HVO command in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see two signatures on the bottom of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of those you have said is your signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other signature, whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the signature of Ivan Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that Prosecutor's exhibit 86 can be admitted into evidence. The source of this document, your Honour, is ECMM. Dr. Mujezinovic, if you would kindly read this document into the record, starting at the top and moving down to the bottom. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it is a question that has already been raised. In order to speed up the debate, is it absolutely necessary that it be read? I think that if the parties are agreed, the transcript identifies the exhibit. I think there have been about 100 various documents to be read and if all the parties are agreed -- when there is disagreement over an exhibit then, of course, we will read it. Is everybody agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am in agreement. I would like however certain provisions of this document read because I am going to ask the witness to comment on those provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Dr. Mujezinovic, would you read the second provision of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The civilian representatives of the Croatian and the Muslim peoples unanimously declare that no conflict would have arisen in Vitez this time too, were it not for the influence of global politics and military operations coming from outside our municipality."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, could you please comment on that particular provision you have just read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Point 2 regarding extraneous influence but the Croatian Democratic Community and the HVO were local institutions and they were deeply involved in all these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, will you turn to the third provision and please read that into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Since many people have already been killed, wounded and captured, we request that the military commanders act in accordance with international humanitarian standards as soon as possible." That is all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, Dr. Mujezinovic, did the military commanders of the HVO act in accordance with international humanitarian standards as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please explain your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not present at the talks in Vitez. The Commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic, and the Chief of Staff of the HVO, Petkovic Milivoj came to Vitez, and the exchange of the captured and killed was agreed on the principle of all for all. However the HVO did not respect this but 13 prominent Muslims from Vitez were transferred to the prison in Busovaca. Among them was the President of the government of Vitez, Mr. Fuad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the other people who were also transferred intellectuals in the Muslim community of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The others either left Vitez afterwards or were displaced and as far as I know they were taken to dig trenches and to fortify HVO lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: of those 13 people, Dr. Mujezinovic, were those people who were leaders of the Muslim community in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that 13 people were not immediately released by the HVO but were instead sent to Busovaca prison. My question to you is: were those 13 people who were leaders in the Muslim community? Were they intellectuals; were they professional people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what other respects, Dr. Mujezinovic, did the military commanders of the HVO not act in accordance with international humanitarian standards as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I asked for assistance at work, I knew that we had a doctor doing surgery specialisation, Zdravko Murica, Dr. Pavkovic who was specialising in anesthesiology, and I asked that a medical student, Mulahalilovic Amar be released, and I asked Dr. Bruno to do this. All three were brought in captivity, and the medical student, who was in his final years -- his hands were bloody from trench-digging. He told me that people who were captured were being taken to the front lines to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people also expelled from the Vitez municipality by the HVO after this document was signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Dr. Mujezinovic, if you would turn to point 4 of this particular document and read that into the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Both sides agree that in Vitez and Province 10, the Vance/Owen plan should be implemented even before it is signed by the Serbian side. Also the army command shall retain their structure in conformity with the ethnic composition of the province and the municipality."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What comments do you have about that provision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That provision had been agreed on in Geneva, and at the local level we had no right nor was it our duty to sign this particular provision before any agreement was reached because we did not know what the results of those negotiations were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, what was done with this particular document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document was repeatedly shown on the local TV programme in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you signed this document, what happened to Mr. Santic and Mr. Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They left the room and Boro Jozic told us that all of us had to go down into the basement, and then Zvonko Cilic came back and told me that I should not go to the basement, that there were many wounded and I had to go back to work at the health centre, and I was taken there again by the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question about this document, Prosecutor's exhibit 86: was this document signed by you freely and voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was ordered to sign it, to sign everything. In fact I was threatened to do it, and I was told also by phone from the command of the Third Corps that I should sign everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic, after you signed this document, were you taken back to the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, tell me what occurred at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a great deal to do there, indeed, and I already told you that I had asked Dr. Bruno to bring some doctors to work, which he actually did, and the three that I mentioned came to work. The staff working there, especially the doctors, were very young and inexperienced. We worked in the best possible way; whoever was wounded we extended medical aid, I personally made a selection if somebody needed to be transferred to Travnik or to Zenica, and some were also transferred to Split. I made the proposals and they were transferred by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of those doctors you had summoned was a medical student; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mulahalilovic Amar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his condition when he came to the health centre to work with you and the other doctors?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The question has been asked and answered, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me get the translation, first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, allow the President to regulate the technical problems. What happened, you did not hear the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I did not hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The question will be put again. I also asked for a question to be repeated, so please repeat the question and you will hear the answer. Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the question of the medical student who came to the hospital to work with the other doctors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mulahalilovic was devoted regarding the wounded, and I asked him why he spent so much time over the wounded and then he showed me his hands and they were all bloody and I asked how come, and he said it was from trench-digging. He had never done any digging before, and his whole palms were full of bloody blisters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you treat any soldiers who had accents that were from outside the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly explain that, if you would?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In our health centre, there were troops coming whom I did not know. They were not from Vitez, because I knew more or less the whole domestic population. I did not ask them where they were from. They had a different accent than the one we have in Vitez. I said that we acted as professionals, treating everybody. If somebody needed surgery, they were sent to the medical centres in Zenica, Travnik, and a part of them to Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you made enquiry of any HVO soldier prior to April 16th about soldiers from outside the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion, in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was some time in January. I do not remember exactly the date. A young man, an HVO soldier, came for me to examine him. There were three soldiers with him who had a different accent, so I asked him, "Who are they?", and he said, "Never mind, doctor, we come from all over the place, from Daruvar, Virovitica" and he told me his ID card, "My command is in Split." I did not check the card.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What country is Split in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to continue my examination of Dr. Mujezinovic, but I would ask that we be permitted to go into private session. I have only a brief additional part of my examination and there are parts of this that are extremely sensitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Private session, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, we will have a private session. Mr. Registrar, will you please make the arrangements? It is all right. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Pages 1726 to 1731 in closed session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo. Cross-examined by MR. NOBILO

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We thank you because you make our work easier. I shall question the witness first in continuity and then my colleague Mr. Hayman will continue. Dr. Mujezinovic, to go back a bit now to 1990, before 1990 in Yugoslavia, in Bosnia, could people freely express their political views outside those coordinates that were set by the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not desirable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible to express political views and to organise oneself freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, according to the rules of that party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could parties be established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean national parties?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any kind of parties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then say that in 1990 the first free elections were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did this party have an assembly of its own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this assembly elect its President and other executive organs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I did not attend that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that it was registered in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes; I did not see their registration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was it carried out in Vitez? Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, as a citizen of Vitez who knew a lot of people there, what were the results of that referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The population of Vitez, of Bosnian and Croat nationality, voted in a large percentage for a sovereign independent Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are now reaching the point of the Crisis Staff. Can you tell me which is the body that founded it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two national parties, the Croat Democratic Community and the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what were the legal grounds for establishing that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Varupa Midhat, a lawyer, said on that occasion that for that there are no legal grounds, but in a situation of war, as he explained it, according to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a War Presidency could be established, not a Crisis Staff. That is the explanation that was given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Croats and Serbs in Vitez, did they believe that this Crisis Staff was a legal or an illegal body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A legal body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, in the morning you talked about that soldier of the BH-Army in the hotel Vitez, and orders came from Travnik to carry out an investigation. I am interested in hearing who submitted the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the Crisis Staff, it was concluded that an investigation should be carried out on this murder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was an inquest carried out and other investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, Vlado Miskovic, the Investigating Prosecutor of the municipal court in Travnik, was entrusted with that task. The results of that investigation have not been completed, to the best of my knowledge. Only Vlado Miskovic, who is from the village of Krisancevo Selo, I think, from Vitez -- he is employed in the court in Travnik as Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Hakija Cenjic as the Commander of the Territorial Defence at the beginning. When did he stop being the Commander of the Territorial Defence in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He stopped being that some time in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the reason why he ceased being Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain what it was about, what was the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Hakija Cenjic is a teacher of physics in the high school and a reserve major of the former army. He asked me, as a doctor, to withdraw. He said that I should withdraw, that he should withdraw, rather, that he should get an easier job, Mr. Cenjic Hakija. I sent him for further examinations to a well known institute in Zagreb, Dr. Skrabalo, the best known institute for diabetes and metabolism illnesses. From the institute where he worked is also Mr. Granic. The current Foreign Minister of Croatia also used to work there, so treatment with insulin was suggested to him there. Perhaps I should not be saying what his illness is, but you do have his evidence that he was a patient in Zagreb and what suggestions were made to him, and physically he simply could not take all of this. Mr. Hakija Cenjic -- as I had suggested to the Executive Board of the party that they put up a new candidate. He personally thanked me for doing that as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not expect too many medical details. Please, just tell me: what is the body that relieved him of this duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The district staff of the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At whose proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the proposal of the Executive Board of the SDA in Vitez because he himself was a member of that body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was elected to replace him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Sefkija Djidic was elected to replace him who at that time was the head of the TO staff in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who proposed Mr. Djidic and who elected him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Executive Board of the SDA from Vitez was looking for a suitable candidate who had professional qualifications. Sefkija Djidic at that time was a reserve first class captain and a teacher of physical education. He was born in Vitez and he knew Vitez very very well. At that point in time, we thought that Sefkija Djidic would truly do everything to prevent a conflict from breaking out in Vitez because he knew everyone in Vitez very well and everything in Vitez very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Executive Board proposed that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They only presented the proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who elected him, who appointed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The district staff of the TO in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Ivica Santic asked Fuad Kaknjo to go back to his job as President of the managing board after the incident when the soldiers came into the police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Fuad Kaknjo respond to that invitation; did he continue working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this incident occurred, when these flags were hoisted and when the army broke in, and you also said that Santic was absent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what we were told by Fuad Kaknjo after Ivica Santic called him. He was away on business; he was not in Vitez at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to know: that evening, that night when that happened, did Fuad Kaknjo convene a meeting of the Crisis Staff? Were you there at that meeting on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not convene a meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who broke into the police station and the municipal building, who exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
